question: Which histone mutations have been associated with pediatric gliomas?

supports.quote: It has been reported recently that about 80% of DIPG cases and 70% of midline glioblastomas contain a mutation at one allele of the H3F3A gene (encoding histone H3 variant H3.3), replacing the lysine 27 with methionine (K27M).
Recent studies on high-grade pediatric GBM have identified two recurrent mutations (K27M and G34R/V) in genes encoding histone H3 (H3F3A for H3.3 and HIST1H3B for H3.1)

initial_executor.limitations: Evidence primarily focuses on high-grade pediatric gliomas (DIPG, GBM). While H3F3A and HIST1H3B are the genes identified, the specific mutation combinations (K27M vs G34R/V) are often associated with specific tumor locations (midline vs hemispheric) and ages, though the evidence provided does not explicitly detail every location-specific constraint for every mutation variant in a single sentence. Some evidence mentions H3.2K27M (e35) but does not explicitly link it to pediatric gliomas in the same context as H3.3.

same_evidence_Qwen.limitations: Evidence primarily focuses on high-grade pediatric gliomas, DIPG, and brainstem tumors; some mutations (G34R/V) are noted in older children/young adults or hemispheric HGGs. Gene names (H3F3A, HIST1H3B) and protein variants (H3.3, H3.1, H3.2) are distinguished based on specific evidence segments. Some evidence mentions 'HIST3H1B' while others mention 'HIST1H3B' for H3.1; both are included as per source text variations.
